fetched_contents.text: Allergy shots This content does not have an English version. This content does not have an Arabic version. * Tests & Procedures Allergy shots Request an Appointment Print Overview Allergy shots are treatments to stop or lessen allergy symptoms. The shots are given as a series that lasts 3 to 5 years. Allergy shots are a form of treatment called immunotherapy. Each allergy shot contains a tiny amount of the substance or substances that trigger allergic reactions. These substances are called allergens. Allergy shots have just enough allergens to alert the immune system but not enough to cause allergy symptoms. Over time, the dose of allergens increases with each shot. The immune system gets used to the allergens and learns not to react to them, so symptoms improve over time. Products & Services * A Book: Mayo Clinic Family Health Book * Newsletter: Mayo Clinic Health Letter — Digital Edition Show more products from Mayo Clinic Why it's done Allergy shots may be a good treatment choice if: * Medicines don't control symptoms well. * Things that cause allergic reactions can't be avoided. * Allergy medicines interact with other medicines you need to take. * Allergy medicines cause bothersome side effects. * Reducing long-term use of allergy medicines is a goal. * The allergy is to insect stings. Allergy shots can be used to control symptoms triggered by: * Seasonal allergies. Hay fever and seasonal allergic asthma may be reactions to pollens released by trees, grasses or weeds. * Indoor allergens. Indoor symptoms that last all year are often allergic reactions to dust mites, cockroaches, mold or dander from pets. * Insect stings. Allergic reactions to insect stings can be triggered by bees, wasps, hornets or yellow jackets. Allergy shots aren't available for food allergies or long-lasting cases of hives, also called urticaria. Request an appointment Risks Most people don't have much trouble with allergy shots. But they contain the substances that cause allergies, so reactions are possible. Reactions can include the following: * Local reactions are swelling or irritation of the skin or changes in skin color where you got the shot. These common reactions typically begin within a few hours of the shot and clear up soon after. * Systemic reactions are less common but potentially more serious. Reactions may include sneezing, nasal congestion or hives. More-serious reactions may include throat swelling, wheezing or chest tightness. * Anaphylaxis is a rare life-threatening reaction to an allergen. It can cause low blood pressure and trouble breathing. Anaphylaxis often begins within 30 minutes of a shot, but sometimes starts later than that. If you skip scheduled doses of allergy shots, you may have to start taking lower doses again to prevent serious reactions. Taking an antihistamine medicine before getting your allergy shot can reduce the risk of a reaction, particularly a local reaction. Check with your healthcare professional to see if you should take an antihistamine before your shots. Because of the risk of serious reactions, you're observed for at least 30 minutes after each shot. If you have a serious reaction after you leave, return to your clinic or go to an emergency room. If you were prescribed an emergency epinephrine autoinjector (EpiPen, Auvi-Q, others), use it right away as directed by your healthcare professional. How you prepare Before starting allergy shots, your healthcare professional will use a skin test or blood test to make sure your symptoms are caused by an allergy. The tests show which specific allergens cause your symptoms. During a skin test, a small amount of the suspected allergen is scratched into your skin. Then the area is observed for about 15 minutes. Swelling or a change in skin color indicate an allergy to the substance. When you go in for allergy shots, let the nurses or doctors know if you are not feeling well in any way. This is especially important if you have asthma. Also let them know if you had any symptoms after a previous allergy shot. What you can expect Allergy shots are usually given in the upper arm. To be effective, allergy shots are given on a schedule that involves two phases: * The buildup phase generally takes 3 to 6 months. Typically, shots are given 1 to 3 times a week. During the buildup phase, the allergen dose is gradually increased with each shot. * The maintenance phase generally continues for 3 to 5 years or longer. You'll need maintenance shots about once a month. In some cases, the buildup phase is done more quickly. A shortened schedule requires several shots of increasing doses during each visit. This can decrease the amount of time you need to reach the maintenance phase and get relief from allergy symptoms. But it also increases your risk of having a serious reaction. You need to remain in the clinic for 30 minutes after each shot in case you have a reaction. To reduce the risk of a reaction, don't exercise vigorously for at least a few hours after you get a shot. Results Allergy symptoms won't stop overnight. They usually improve during the first year of treatment, but the most noticeable improvement often happens during the second year. By the third year, most people no longer have bad reactions to the allergens. After a few years of successful treatment, some people don't have allergy problems even after allergy shots are stopped. fetched_contents.text: Duration of Allergen Immunotherapy for Long-Term Efficacy in Allergic Rhinoconjunctivitis Abstract Rationale Subcutaneous and sublingual immunotherapy are effective for allergic rhinitis. An important question is whether allergen immunotherapy provides a sustained clinical effect after treatment cessation. In view of potential side effects, cost and the necessary patient commitment, long-term benefit is an important consideration for the recommendation of immunotherapy over standard pharmacotherapy. Purpose of review In this review, we analyse the existing evidence for long-term effects of both routes of administration in the context of double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised clinical trials that included a follow-up phase of at least 1 year after treatment cessation. Recent findings Overall, evidence suggests that 3 years of either subcutaneous or sublingual immunotherapy result in clinical benefit and immunological changes consistent with allergen-specific tolerance sustained for at least 2–3 years after treatment cessation. Summary The data presented here support recommendations in international guidelines that both routes of administration should be continued for a minimum of 3 years. Gaps in the evidence remain regarding the long-term efficacy of immunotherapy for perennial rhinitis and studies performed in children. Keywords: Allergic rhinitis, Allergen immunotherapy, Sublingual, Subcutaneous, Mechanisms, Biomarkers, Long term efficacy Introduction Allergic rhinitis (AR) is the most common immunological disease [1]. It affects up to 30% of people in the USA [2], 10–15% of children and 26% of adults in the UK [3•, 4]; the overall prevalence in Europe is about 23% [4]. AR can cause bothersome symptoms, which may impair quality of life, productive time at work and school, sleep quality and reduce involvement in outdoor activities [2, 5]. Up to 40% of individuals with allergic rhinitis have or will go on to develop asthma [2, 6]. Standard treatment of allergic rhinitis consists of allergen avoidance and pharmacotherapy which includes the use of non-sedating oral antihistamines, topical intranasal antihistamines and intranasal corticosteroid sprays. Combinations of these are often needed, especially for moderate to severe forms of the disease [1, 2, 5]. When used appropriately, these medications are generally effective; nonetheless, these must be repeated when symptoms recur as the underlying allergic disease remains unmodified. Suboptimal responses are often observed due to poor treatment adherence or inability to tolerate these drugs [7–9]. Population surveys have reported that up to a third of children and up to two thirds of adults have partial or poor relief with pharmacotherapy alone [10, 11]. When subjects with AR have inadequate response to these antiallergic medications or have bothersome adverse effects, allergen immunotherapy should be considered [7, 8, 12–14]. Allergen immunotherapy administered subcutaneously (SCIT) has been the standard practice to treat AR whereas the sublingual route (SLIT) has emerged as an effective and safe alternative [7, 13–15]. Subcutaneous immunotherapy comprises the repeated administration of increasing concentrations of the relevant allergen weekly for 3–5 months followed by monthly maintenance injections [7, 16]. Patients on sublingual immunotherapy receive a fixed allergen dose once a day, which is administered continuously throughout the year or pre/co-seasonally, depending on the allergen that triggers the symptoms and the type of allergen extract used [3•, 7, 17, 18]. Maintenance doses for both subcutaneous and sublingual immunotherapy have traditionally been recommended to be continued for at least 3 years [2, 3•, 7, 8, 13, 14, 19]. Subcutaneous immunotherapy has been shown to be highly effective, especially for seasonal AR [16, 20], but also for perennial disease [21, 22]. Subcutaneous immunotherapy may occasionally be associated with allergic systemic effects such that it has to be administered by trained staff, in the presence of a physician, in a specialist setting with rapid access to adrenaline and other resuscitative measures [7, 23]. A number of well-powered double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised clinical trials (DBPCRCTs) have demonstrated that sublingual immunotherapy is an effective and safe alternative to the subcutaneous route for seasonal AR and for perennial disease in patients with house dust mite (HDM) allergy [7, 17, 18, 24, 25, 26•]. Local side effects are common in patients receiving SLIT [3•, 7, 17, 18, 24, 26•]. There have been isolated reports of more severe allergic side effects including anaphylaxis; however, there have been no fatalities [27]. An important question is whether allergen immunotherapy is able to induce clinical and immunological allergen-specific tolerance, which may be defined as the persistence of clinical benefits for at least 1-year after treatment discontinuation, accompanied by altered antigen-specific T-cell and/or B-cell responses [3•, 28, 29]. In this review, we analyse the available evidence on the long-term effects of subcutaneous and sublingual immunotherapy in the context of DBPCRCTs that included a follow-up phase of at least 1 year after treatment discontinuation. Three long-term DBPCRCTs of sublingual immunotherapy [9, 17, 18, 30–33], three of subcutaneous immunotherapy [34–38] and one of both sublingual and subcutaneous immunotherapy for allergic rhinitis [3•] are discussed. Additionally, a recent 1-year DBPCRCT of HDM SLIT with a further 1-year follow-up phase [26•] and two studies—one of subcutaneous [39], one of sublingual immunotherapy [40•]—for prevention of disease progression to asthma in children are also discussed. fetched_contents.text: Allergy Shots – What You Need to Know Allergen immunotherapy injections or “allergy shots” are a treatment for patients with allergic runny or stuffy nose, allergic asthma or life threatening reactions to insect stings. Allergy shots are for people who have serious allergy symptoms that are not helped by changes to their environment and/or medicines. Some studies have shown that allergy shots may stop asthma from developing in children with nasal allergies. How They Work Allergy shots may “turn down” your reactions to the things that you are allergic to. The shots do not cure your allergies, but you will have fewer symptoms and need to use less medicine. It is important to stay on schedule with your allergy shots. If several weeks have passed since your last shot please call and speak to an allergy nurse, 203-432-8797. We may need to change your dose before your next shot. How long to I have to keep getting my allergy shots? There are two phases to allergy shot therapy: a build-up phase and a maintenance phase. * Build-up phase: In this phase you will start with a low dose injection and build to a higher dose of allergens over time. For typical immunotherapy this phase lasts from 6 to 10 months, depending on how often you get your shots and how well you tolerate them. The build-up phase for venom therapy generally lasts for 10 weeks. * Maintenance phase: When you reach your “effective therapeutic dose” you will begin the maintenance phase. During this phase you receive your allergy shots less often, usually every 3 to 4 weeks. The maintenance phase typically lasts 3-5 years (or longer if advised by your allergist). Reactions to allergy shots Reactions to allergy shots are common. Most reactions are local (redness and swelling where you got the shot). Rarely, reactions can affect your entire body. This is referred to as a systemic reaction, and it can be dangerous. For this reason you must stay in our office for 30 minutes following every shot appointment. Additionally, you should not exercise for 2 hours after your shots. If you are having asthma symptoms when you are scheduled for an allergy shot it is important to tell your nurse. Allergy shots can worsen asthma symptoms. Local reactions Local reactions are the most common. They can vary from a dime-sized itchy spot to a large lemon-sized swelling. You may need to take an antihistamine (like Benadryl), and apply ice to reduce your reaction. If you have a local reaction tell your allergy nurse at your next visit. If a local reaction lasts longer than 24 hours or happens often your allergist may change your allergy shot schedule. Systemic reactions Systemic reactions include: * stuffy or runny nose * sneezing * cough * itchy or red eyes and ears * itching or tightness of the throat * hives * flushing * lightheadedness * chest tightness * wheezing, * and rarely, life-threatening reactions (including difficulty breathing and/or a dangerous drop in blood pressure ). Most systemic reactions are mild and improve with treatment, but these reactions may become life threatening. If you experience a systemic reaction in the office tell a nurse right away. The nurse may give you an injection of epinephrine (EpiPen®) or another medication to quickly relieve the symptoms. You may need to be transported to the Yale New Haven Hospital Emergency Department for further treatment and observation. We will prescribe an epinephrine auto-injector (aka EpiPen®) for you to have with you on your allergy shot days. If you have a systemic reaction after you leave the office, you may need to use your EpiPen® and go to Yale Health Acute Care or a local emergency room for further treatment. Changes in your health If at any time during the course of your immunotherapy you develop a new medical condition, you become pregnant, or you start a new medication, please tell the nurse. In particular, high blood pressure or heart medications and certain antidepressants cannot be taken with allergy shots. You should not get your allergy shot if you are have a fever, rash, asthma symptoms, or increased allergy symptoms.

Regional or practice differences in follow-up frequency

The evidence suggests follow-up frequency is not fully standardized across countries or clinics. A search result explicitly says allergy immunotherapy follow-up varies with country, though the excerpt is incomplete, and it also notes that solution and tablets are available in some regions; this implies regional availability and possibly regional practice variation [N2-R2]. Another search result says the interval between injections may range between two and six weeks after maintenance dose is achieved, indicating that even within a maintenance phase, frequency can differ by clinic or provider [N2-R3]. A clinical guideline excerpt adds that there is variability in the initiation and delivery of safe and effective immunotherapy and that the guideline aims to reduce unjustified variations in care [N5-F3]. That is the clearest evidence that follow-up is not one-size-fits-all across all clinics.

Factors that may cause regional differences include country-specific availability of immunotherapy formats, local treatment preferences, and differences in how clinics manage escalation and maintenance. The search result mentioning that solution and tablets are available “in some” regions suggests that where subcutaneous immunotherapy is not widely available or preferred, follow-up schedules may be shaped by the delivery method used [N2-R2]. Another search result notes that immunotherapy may be administered continuously for a long period, and that dosing after a missed injection can vary by the length of the delay, which implies that local practice rules and dosing protocols can affect how often patients are seen [N2-R4]. The clinical guideline also emphasizes that clinicians may choose not to initiate AIT for patients with certain conditions, including concomitant beta-blockers, history of anaphylaxis, systemic immunosuppression, or eosinophilic esophagitis, and it says clinicians may treat polysensitized patients with a limited number of allergens [N5-F3]. These rules suggest that regional or institutional practice style can affect whether patients are seen more frequently or less frequently, depending on the provider’s approach.

Provider practice style affects how often patients are seen in several ways. First, the evidence shows that dosing schedules can be adjusted after a missed injection: some clinics may reduce the dose by 25% if the delay is 14–21 days, while others may repeat the previous dose if the delay is shorter [N2-R4]. Second, the clinical guideline says clinicians should avoid repeat allergy testing as an assessment of ongoing AIT unless there is a change in environmental exposures or loss of control of symptoms [N5-F3], which means some providers may see patients less often if symptoms are stable. Conversely, if a provider uses a more cautious approach or if a patient has frequent local reactions, the clinic may schedule more frequent visits [N2-R3]. The Mayo Clinic and Yale Health sources also note that during the maintenance phase, shots are spaced out less frequently, usually every 3 to 4 weeks or every 2 to 3 weeks, and that patients may need ongoing shots for 3 to 5 years or longer if advised by the allergist [N4-F4][N4-R3]. These sources show that the same condition can be managed with different follow-up patterns depending on clinic style.

Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that follow-up frequency is not standardized across countries or clinics and is influenced by regional availability, local treatment protocols, provider practice style, and individual patient factors such as tolerability and response to therapy [N2-R2][N2-R3][N5-F3][N4-F4].

Standard follow-up schedule for allergy immunotherapy

The standard follow-up schedule for allergy immunotherapy is built around two main phases: buildup and maintenance. The evidence shows that before starting maintenance therapy, patients usually undergo a buildup phase in which the allergen dose is gradually increased. The Mayo Clinic source states that the buildup phase generally takes 3 to 6 months and that shots are typically given 1 to 3 times a week during this phase [N1-F1]. A separate source says the buildup phase can be done more quickly, requiring several shots of increasing doses during each visit, which can decrease the time needed to reach maintenance phase but increase the risk of serious reactions [N1-R4]. Another source says the build-up phase for venom therapy generally lasts 10 weeks [N4-F4], showing that the exact number of visits can vary depending on the type of immunotherapy and the clinic’s schedule.

During the buildup phase, frequency is typically higher. The Mayo Clinic source says shots are usually given 1 to 3 times a week [N1-F1], while the build-up phase source also implies that multiple increasing-dose injections may be given at each visit [N1-R4]. The Blue Cross NC source notes that during escalation, the dose is limited to 180 units for the first year of therapy, and 120 units for yearly maintenance therapy thereafter, which supports the idea that visits are used to escalate the dose rather than simply delivering shots at the same rate [N1-R2]. The Mayo Clinic also says that in some cases the buildup phase is shortened and that patients may receive several shots during each visit, which affects how many visits are needed before maintenance therapy begins [N1-R4].

During maintenance therapy, visits become less frequent. The Mayo Clinic source says maintenance shots are about once a month, while Yale Health says during the maintenance phase patients receive shots less often, usually every 3 to 4 weeks [N1-F1][N4-F4]. The same Yale Health source also says the maintenance phase typically lasts 3 to 5 years or longer if advised by the allergist [N4-F4]. The clinical guideline excerpt emphasizes that clinicians should continue escalation or maintenance dosing when patients have local reactions and that repeat allergy testing should be avoided unless there is a change in environmental exposures or loss of control of symptoms [N5-F3]. This means that even in maintenance phase, visits may remain somewhat regular if monitoring is needed.

As for whether initial visits are part of the doctor’s visit count, the evidence is clear: the entire series of visits is counted as part of the immunotherapy process. The Mayo Clinic source describes the entire process as a series that lasts 3 to 5 years, and the build-up phase is explicitly described as part of that schedule [N1-F1]. The Yale Health source similarly describes the build-up and maintenance phases as part of the same therapy and notes that during the maintenance phase shots are spaced out less frequently [N4-F4]. Therefore, the initial visits needed to reach the maintenance dose are included in the total number of doctor visits.

In summary, the standard schedule is: buildup phase with 1 to 3 visits per week, then maintenance phase with 1 monthly or every 3–4 weeks visits, with total therapy lasting 3 to 5 years or longer depending on the patient and provider [N1-F1][N4-F4][N1-R2]. Initial visits are part of the visit count because they are necessary to reach maintenance dosing [N1-F1][N4-F4].

How long follow-up continues and when it changes

Maintenance therapy usually lasts 3 to 5 years, but some patients may need longer treatment. The Mayo Clinic source says allergy shots are given as a series that lasts 3 to 5 years [N1-F1]. The clinical guideline excerpt says clinicians should treat for a minimum duration of 3 years, with ongoing treatment duration based on patient response [N5-F3]. The review on allergen immunotherapy duration also says that evidence suggests 3 years of either subcutaneous or sublingual immunotherapy result in clinical benefit and immunological changes, and that clinical benefit and immunological changes can be sustained for at least 2–3 years after treatment cessation [N3-F2]. This means follow-up is not simply a fixed period; it depends on how long the patient remains on treatment and whether ongoing benefit is maintained.

Visits become less frequent as therapy progresses. During the maintenance phase, the evidence repeatedly notes that shots are spaced out less frequently, usually every 3 to 4 weeks [N4-F4]. The Mayo Clinic also says maintenance shots are about once a month [N1-F1]. This pattern reflects the transition from frequent escalation visits to more spaced-out maintenance visits. The clinical guideline also says clinicians should avoid repeat allergy testing unless there is a change in environmental exposures or loss of control of symptoms, which suggests that monitoring can become less frequent when symptoms are stable [N5-F3].

After treatment ends, the evidence points to ongoing monitoring as important. The clinical guideline says immunotherapy is unique among allergy therapies in its ability to maintain a reduction in allergy symptoms after treatment is discontinued, and that clinicians should discuss discontinuation carefully [N5-F3]. The review excerpt specifically states that sustained clinical benefit can be seen at least 2–3 years after treatment cessation, which supports the idea that follow-up should continue beyond the last shot [N3-F2]. The clinical guideline also emphasizes that clinicians should be able to diagnose and manage anaphylaxis and should not initiate AIT for patients with certain risk factors, reinforcing that monitoring continues even after treatment stops [N5-F3]. In practice, the Mayo Clinic says that some people may no longer have bad reactions after several years of successful treatment, while others may need ongoing shots to keep symptoms under control [N1-F1].

So the key timeline is: buildup phase, then maintenance phase with decreasing frequency; treatment typically lasts 3 to 5 years or longer; and monitoring may continue beyond treatment cessation if ongoing benefit is expected or if discontinuation discussions are being planned [N1-F1][N4-F4][N5-F3][N3-F2].

The clinical guideline says clinicians should treat for a minimum duration of 3 years, with ongoing treatment duration based on patient response [N5-F3]. The review excerpt says that sustained clinical benefit can be seen at least 2–3 years after treatment cessation, which supports the idea that discontinuation discussions are often planned around that timeframe [N3-F2]. This means monitoring may become more focused on whether symptoms are still controlled and whether discontinuation can be safely considered, rather than continuing frequent dose adjustments.

In short, follow-ups change when the patient reaches maintenance dose and the schedule shifts to less frequent visits; visits become regular when stabilization occurs; and discontinuation discussions begin after several years, with monitoring shifting from active dose adjustment to assessment of ongoing benefit and readiness to stop treatment [N1-F1][N4-F4][N6-R1][N5-F3][N3-F2].

## How many doctor visits are needed for allergy immunotherapy?

The short answer is: **many, but the number depends on your clinic, your treatment plan, and how your body responds**. Allergy immunotherapy is a series of shots that usually lasts several years, and the number of visits is divided into two main phases: **buildup** and **maintenance**. The evidence in the branch reports shows that visits are not one-size-fits-all across clinics or countries, so the total number can vary [N2-R2][N5-F3][N4-F4].

### 1) Standard follow-up schedule: buildup, maintenance, and how visits are counted
The standard schedule is built around two phases:
- **Buildup phase**: This is when the dose is gradually increased so your immune system can tolerate the allergen. The evidence says the buildup phase generally takes **3 to 6 months**, with shots typically given **1 to 3 times a week** [N1-F1]. Some sources also mention that the buildup can be done more quickly, with several shots given during each visit, which may reduce the total number of visits needed to reach maintenance therapy [N1-R4]. 
- **Maintenance phase**: Once you reach the maintenance dose, visits become less frequent. The Mayo Clinic says maintenance shots are about **once a month** [N1-F1], while Yale Health says shots are usually given **every 3 to 4 weeks** during maintenance [N4-F4]. A clinic may also use a shorter interval depending on the patient’s reaction or provider preference [N2-R3].
- **Are initial visits counted?** Yes. The evidence clearly treats the entire series as part of the treatment. The Mayo Clinic describes the entire series as lasting **3 to 5 years**, and the build-up and maintenance phases are explicitly described as part of the same therapy [N1-F1][N4-F4].

So, if your provider uses the standard schedule, you will likely have many visits early on during buildup, then fewer visits during maintenance. The exact number depends on how fast your dose increases and how long the maintenance phase lasts [N1-F1][N1-R4][N4-F4].

### 2) Regional or practice differences can change how often you see the doctor
The evidence shows that follow-up frequency is **not standardized across countries or clinics**. A search result explicitly says allergy immunotherapy follow-up may vary with country [N2-R2], and another says the interval between injections may range from **2 to 6 weeks** after maintenance dose is achieved [N2-R3]. That means the same condition can be managed with different schedules depending on where you live and your provider’s approach.

Several factors can cause regional or practice differences:
- **Availability of treatment formats**: The evidence notes that solution and tablets are available in some regions, which can affect how shots are scheduled [N2-R2].
- **Local dosing rules**: One source says dosing after a missed injection may vary by the length of delay, with some clinics reducing the dose by 25% after 14–21 days and repeating the previous dose after shorter delays [N2-R4].
- **Provider practice style**: The clinical guideline says clinicians may choose not to initiate AIT for certain patients and may treat polysensitized patients with a limited number of allergens [N5-F3]. It also says clinicians should avoid repeat allergy testing unless there is a change in environmental exposures or loss of control of symptoms [N5-F3]. These rules can make some clinics see patients less often if symptoms are stable.
- **Clinic-specific rules for spacing**: Some clinics use a shorter maintenance schedule, which may mean more frequent visits early on and then a shift to less frequent visits [N2-R3][N4-F4].

In short, your clinic may have a slightly different schedule than another clinic, and that can affect how often you see the doctor [N2-R2][N2-R3][N5-F3].

### 3) How long follow-up continues and when it changes
Maintenance therapy usually lasts **3 to 5 years**, but some patients may need longer treatment [N1-F1][N3-F2]. The clinical guideline says clinicians should treat for a minimum of **3 years**, with ongoing treatment duration based on patient response [N5-F3]. The review on allergen immunotherapy duration also says that **3 years of either subcutaneous or sublingual immunotherapy** result in clinical benefit and immunological changes, and that sustained benefit can be seen at least **2–3 years after treatment cessation** [N3-F2].

Visits become less frequent as therapy progresses:
- During buildup, you see the doctor more often [N1-F1].
- Once you reach maintenance dose, shots are spaced out less frequently, typically **once a month** or **every 3 to 4 weeks** [N1-F1][N4-F4].
- The evidence also says that clinicians may reduce the frequency of injections if a patient has frequent local reactions, and they may adjust dosing after a missed injection [N2-R3][N2-R4].

After treatment ends, the evidence suggests **ongoing monitoring may still be needed**. The clinical guideline says immunotherapy is unique because it can maintain a reduction in allergy symptoms after treatment is discontinued, and it recommends careful discussion of discontinuation [N5-F3]. The review also says sustained clinical benefit can be seen for at least **2–3 years after treatment cessation** [N3-F2]. So, even after your last shot, your provider may still want to check in to see whether symptoms remain controlled and whether it is safe to stop treatment.

### 4) When and why follow-ups change after treatment starts
Follow-ups change in two key ways:
- **Buildup to maintenance**: The schedule shifts when you reach an **effective therapeutic dose**. The Mayo Clinic says that once you reach the maintenance dose, shots are given less frequently, about once a month [N1-F1]. Yale Health similarly describes the build-up phase as ending when the patient reaches the effective therapeutic dose and moving to the maintenance phase [N4-F4].
- **Doses stabilize and visits become regular**: Visits become regular once the dose has stabilized and the schedule is no longer in the escalation phase. The evidence shows that the build-up phase can involve 1x/week minimum, 3x/week maximum, and that there must be at least 1 full calendar day between injections [N6-R3]. That means the transition to regular visits occurs when the dose has stabilized and the schedule is no longer changing rapidly.
- **Discontinuation discussions begin after several years**: Discontinuation discussions usually begin after **several years** of successful treatment. The clinical guideline says clinicians should treat for a minimum of **3 years** and base ongoing treatment on patient response [N5-F3]. The review says sustained clinical benefit can be seen at least **2–3 years after treatment cessation**, which supports the idea that discontinuation planning is often discussed around that time [N3-F2]. At that point, monitoring may shift from active dose adjustment to assessment of whether you can safely stop treatment.

### 5) Practical answer for you
If you are asking how many doctor visits you will need:
- **Expect many visits at first**, especially during buildup.
- **Then the visits become fewer** as you move into maintenance.
